blocks.text: Charles Olson joins the firm this month as a Design Technician. He is an experienced hand, and he will draft across the board as the work requires, setting up new sheets to the layout each recurring client prefers.

Charles works in the engineering group and reports to Linda George, Project Engineer. Linda will fit him to the jobs where his experience counts most. He knows the older conventions of the board and keeps to the firm's established way of laying out a set, which is worth more than a shortcut when a client expects its plans to look the way they always have. Several of the firm's clients have had their plans arranged the same way for years, and they notice at once when a sheet departs from it; Charles is the kind of hand who keeps that continuity without being asked.

The practical side is short. His station is on the CAD network, the standard-detail library and the client sheet setups live under the lettered project folders, and time is kept by project number on the weekly sheet. The review order holds for every set: the drawings are checked and the cover sheet is sealed before anything is issued. Charles has worked to that discipline for years and needs no instruction in it. Where a client's preferred layout is not written down, he should note it so the next technician has it in hand. He should also look over the standard-detail library with an eye for details that have fallen out of date, and mark any he finds for an engineer to review before they are used again.
For a first assignment, Linda George will put him on one of the recurring-client sets, where his memory for how each likes its plans laid out is of immediate use.
